cultivar: Sichuan small- and medium-leaf population from Mengding
processing: Made as several classes at one state-founded farm: green, black and white teas, plus Tibetan-style brick tea, some of it still dried over firewood.
harvest_season: Spring is the usual picking for the class; one report places picking at the farm in May.
appearance_dry: The green tea is typically fine twisted leaf in a mid green, as with other Sichuan-derived greens.
appearance_liquor: Typical of Chinese greens, a clear yellow-green.
appearance_wet: Typically small to medium green leaf, as is usual for this Sichuan plant stock.
taste_profile: No detailed tasting notes are firmly documented; the green tea can be expected to run fresh and gently sweet, as with other high-altitude Chinese greens.

brewing.notes: General advice for a Chinese green: start around 85 degrees and adjust by taste. The farm's black and brick teas take boiling water.

vintage_note: The green tea is sold as the current year's harvest, in the farm's graded series such as Select and Premium. Black, white and brick teas from the same farm follow their own classes, and the name Yigong on a pack does not tell you which is inside, so check.
description:
Yigong Tea comes from a single place, the Yigong Tea Farm in Bomê county, Nyingchi, in southeastern Tibet. It sits around 2,280 metres. The surprise is the location: tea growing at scale on the Tibetan side of these mountains.

The plants are not native. They are Sichuan small- and medium-leaf bushes from the Mengding area, brought in by the army farm that started here. Today the farm makes green, black and white teas, plus Tibetan-style brick tea, some of it dried over firewood.

Reliable tasting notes are scarce. Treat the green as you would a good Sichuan green, with water around 85 degrees and short steeps, and judge for yourself.

When buying, read the label closely, since one name covers very different teas. The farm brands include Yigong Tea Farm and Xueyu Chagu.
history:
The farm began as a military reclamation project, with tea introduced from Sichuan around 1960. Accounts differ in detail: one dates the first planting to 1960, another gives the farm's founding as 1961 and the arrival of Mengding seed as 1964. All agree on the Sichuan origin.

It was renamed Yigong Tea Farm in 1993, and renovation became a Tibet aid project from 1994. After a long run of losses, a Guangdong aid team began upgrading it in 2019. The farm recorded its first profit in 2020 and made its first export in 2021.
